nameStory: The 'ebony' in this damselfly's name comes from the males' striking jet-black wings that shimmer like polished wood. The 'jewelwing' part describes how their dark wings catch and reflect light like precious gems, creating an almost metallic sheen as they flutter along streams.
description: The Ebony Jewelwing is a broad-winged damselfly that's quite different from the typical thin-winged damselflies you might know. Males sport dramatically wide, coal-black wings that make them look more like tiny dark butterflies than typical damselflies. Females have smoky brown wings with distinctive white spots near the tips. These damselflies are medium-sized insects that fold their wings back along their body when at rest, unlike dragonflies which hold their wings outstretched.

idTips.label: Male wing color
idTips.description: Males have completely jet-black wings with a metallic green or blue sheen that shifts as they move in the light - no other damselfly in New England has wings this dark

idTips.label: Female wing markings
idTips.description: Females have smoky brown wings with bright white patches near the wing tips that look like someone dabbed white paint on them

idTips.label: Wing width
idTips.description: Wings are noticeably broader than typical damselflies - about twice as wide as a bluet's wings and feel more substantial if you gently catch one

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Body is metallic green or blue-black, feeling smooth and cool to touch, with males being more brilliantly colored than females

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with deep, slow wingbeats that create an almost butterfly-like fluttering motion rather than the quick darting of other damselflies

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Males often perch on prominent rocks or logs over water with wings slightly spread, showing off their dark wing patches like tiny flags

habitat: Look for Ebony Jewelwings along clean, flowing streams and small rivers with rocky or gravelly bottoms, especially where there's dappled sunlight filtering through overhanging trees. They prefer areas with good water quality and are often found near riffles and pools where the current varies. You'll spot them perching on rocks, fallen logs, or low vegetation within a few feet of the water's edge.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males appearing first to establish territories along prime stream sections. Look for the first dark-winged males patrolling sunny spots over moving water.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through summer when both males and females are abundant, with territorial males displaying prominently on rocks and logs while females visit water to mate and lay eggs. This is the best time to observe their courtship flights.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, though numbers decline as temperatures cool. Late-season individuals may be more worn, with males' wing colors appearing less intense.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts, spending winter as larvae developing underwater in the stream sediment and under rocks.

funFact: Male Ebony Jewelwings are such show-offs that they'll actually hover in front of females and flash their black wings like tiny semaphore flags, performing an elaborate courtship dance that can last several minutes - and if another male intrudes, they'll engage in aerial 'sword fights' using their wings like miniature dueling blades!
confusionNotes: The dark wings make males unmistakable, but females with their brown wings and white spots might be confused with other broad-winged damselflies. Remember the white wing-tip patches on females - they're like little landing lights that no other damselfly species has in quite the same way.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'jewelwings,' these damselflies belong to a completely different family than the small, bright blue damselflies (bluets) that most people think of as typical damselflies. The broad-winged damselfly family is actually more ancient and primitive than their thin-winged cousins.
compareHints: Among the jewelwing species, Ebony Jewelwings are the only ones where males have completely black wings - River Jewelwings have metallic green wing patches, Sparkling Jewelwings have wings that are only partly darkened, and Superb Jewelwings show brilliant blue-green iridescence. The all-black male wings make Ebony Jewelwings the easiest jewelwing to identify with confidence.

relatedSpecies.distinction: River Jewelwings can be distinguished from Ebony Jewelwings by their preference for larger waterways and slightly different wing coloration patterns.
Superb Jewelwings are distinguished from other New England jewelwings primarily by the male's bright metallic green body color.
Compared to the Ebony Jewelwing, the Sparkling Jewelwing has more extensive metallic green-blue coloration on both wings and body, while Ebony Jewelwings are generally darker overall.
